pharm: Recombinant human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (rHuG-CSF) that stimulates neutrophil precursor proliferation, differentiation, and release from bone marrow.

Not relevant; given by injection, not orally

summary: Lenograstim is a glycosylated recombinant human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (rHuG-CSF) that reduces the duration of neutropenia and the incidence of febrile neutropenia. It is used after cytotoxic chemotherapy for non-myeloid malignancy, after myeloablative therapy followed by bone marrow transplantation, and to mobilize peripheral blood progenitor cells (PBSC) for collection in patients and healthy donors. It is given subcutaneously or by short intravenous infusion at 150 micrograms/m2 (5 micrograms/kg) daily for marrow recovery, or 10 micrograms/kg/day for mobilization. Key safety concerns include rare splenic rupture, capillary leak syndrome, pulmonary reactions including ARDS, and the need to avoid administration concurrently with cytotoxic chemotherapy.
indications: Reduction in the duration of neutropenia in patients undergoing myeloablative therapy followed by bone marrow transplantation
Reduction in the duration of neutropenia and associated febrile neutropenia in patients with non-myeloid malignancy treated with established cytotoxic chemotherapy
Mobilization of peripheral blood progenitor cells (PBSC), alone or after myelosuppressive chemotherapy, in patients and in healthy donors

dosage.n: Start about 24 h after chemotherapy; continue until neutrophils stabilize, max 28 consecutive days
Begin no sooner than 24 h after marrow infusion; continue until neutrophil recovery, max 28 days
Continue through apheresis; timing of leukapheresis guided by CD34+/neutrophil counts
Apheresis typically days 5-7; for healthy donors use only after careful risk evaluation

admin: Reconstitute the powder with the supplied solvent and do not shake vigorously
Give by subcutaneous injection or by short (about 30-minute) intravenous infusion per indication
Do not administer concomitantly with cytotoxic chemotherapy; observe the 24-hour gap after chemotherapy or marrow infusion
Use reconstituted solution immediately or store at 2-8 C for up to 24 hours; do not freeze
moa: Lenograstim is a glycosylated rHuG-CSF produced in mammalian (CHO) cells. It binds to G-CSF receptors on neutrophilic progenitor and mature cells, stimulating proliferation and differentiation of committed neutrophil precursors, accelerating their maturation and release from the bone marrow, and enhancing the functional activity of mature neutrophils. This shortens the duration of chemotherapy- or transplant-induced neutropenia and mobilizes CD34+ hematopoietic progenitor cells into the peripheral blood for collection.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to lenograstim or any excipient
Myeloid malignancy other than de novo acute myeloid leukemia in patients aged 55 years and over
relative: Pre-malignant or malignant myeloid conditions (G-CSF can stimulate cell growth)
Sickle cell disease (risk of sickle cell crisis)
Risk factors for thromboembolism or capillary leak syndrome
monitor: Neutrophil and platelet counts during therapy

preg: There are no adequate data on the use of lenograstim in pregnant women, and animal studies have shown reproductive toxicity. Lenograstim (GRANOCYTE) should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
lact: It is not known whether lenograstim is excreted in human milk; breastfeeding should be discontinued during treatment with lenograstim.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for renal impairment is defined in the labeling; clinical monitoring is advised. Healthy stem-cell donors with significant renal dysfunction generally should not undergo mobilization.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment is defined in the labeling; transient elevations in liver enzymes (ALP, LDH, AST/ALT, GGT) may occur and clinical monitoring is advised.

major: Cytotoxic chemotherapy given concurrently (contraindicated; rapidly dividing myeloid cells are sensitive to cytotoxics, so do not give G-CSF during chemotherapy)
moderate: Other drugs that promote release of neutrophils (e.g., lithium) may potentiate the effect
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with alcohol has been described.
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently increase neutrophil and CD34+ counts, alkaline phosphatase, LDH, and uric acid; bone imaging may show altered marrow uptake. Possible interference with some imaging studies.

common: Transient rise in liver enzymes (ALP, LDH, AST/ALT, GGT)
serious: Capillary leak syndrome (hypotension, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hemoconcentration)
Pulmonary reactions including interstitial pneumonia and ARDS
Sickle cell crisis (in patients with sickle cell disease)
emergency: Splenic rupture (acute left upper quadrant or shoulder-tip pain, hypotension)

monitoring: Full blood count with neutrophil count (regularly during therapy)
Spleen size by examination or imaging
Respiratory signs and symptoms (dyspnea, hypoxia, cough)
Signs of capillary leak syndrome (edema, hypotension)
counsel: Report left upper abdominal or shoulder-tip pain promptly, as it can signal a swollen or ruptured spleen
Report any breathing difficulty, cough, or fever to your care team
Bone pain is common and is usually managed with simple analgesics
Injections are usually given once daily; keep all blood-count appointments
Do not receive this drug at the same time as your chemotherapy infusion
pk: Neutrophil count rises within hours to about 1-2 days of starting therapy
Serum concentration peaks several hours after subcutaneous dosing
Approximately 3 hours (longer, ~2.3-3.3 h, after SC than IV dosing)
Daily dosing required; neutrophil count falls toward baseline within days of stopping
Store below 30 C; do not freeze. Use reconstituted solution immediately or within 24 h at 2-8 C
pearls: Not US FDA-approved; lenograstim (GRANOCYTE) is licensed in the EU/EMA. Use the EMA/SmPC and BNF rather than an FDA prescribing information
Glycosylated rHuG-CSF (essentially a glycosylated counterpart of filgrastim); 150 micrograms/m2 is roughly equivalent to 5 micrograms/kg per day
Never give concurrently with cytotoxic chemotherapy; observe the 24-hour gap after chemotherapy or marrow infusion
Splenic rupture, capillary leak syndrome, and pulmonary toxicity (including ARDS) are rare but can be life-threatening
Use 10 micrograms/kg/day when mobilizing PBSC with G-CSF alone, including in carefully selected healthy donors
missed: This is a once-daily injection usually administered in a clinical setting. If a dose is missed, contact the care team for advice; do not double the next dose. Maintaining the daily schedule is important for neutrophil recovery or stem-cell mobilization.
overdose: The consequences of overdose are not well established. Excessive dosing may cause marked leukocytosis and exacerbate adverse effects such as bone pain or splenomegaly. Management is supportive with discontinuation and monitoring of blood counts (which fall after stopping) and spleen size; there is no specific antidote.
